nameStory: The ski-tipped emerald gets its distinctive name from the unique shape of the male's abdominal appendages, which look remarkably like the curved tips of downhill skis. When viewed from the side, these specialized structures really do resemble tiny skis complete with their characteristic upward curve at the end.
description: The ski-tipped emerald is a medium-sized dragonfly with the brilliant metallic green sheen that gives all emerald dragonflies their name. Like other emeralds, it has a robust body and relatively broad wings that shimmer with an iridescent quality in sunlight. These dragonflies are strong fliers that patrol territories along streams and forest edges, often hovering in place before darting off to catch prey or investigate intruders.

idTips.label: Ski-shaped tail appendages
idTips.description: Males have distinctive curved abdominal appendages that truly look like miniature ski tips when viewed from the side - this is the most reliable field mark

idTips.label: Metallic green body
idTips.description: The thorax and abdomen gleam with a brilliant emerald-green metallic sheen that shifts and changes as the dragonfly moves in the light

idTips.label: Clear wings with amber tinge
idTips.description: Wings are mostly transparent but often show a subtle amber or yellowish wash, especially at the bases, and feel papery-thin to the touch

idTips.label: Patrol flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies in regular patrol routes along stream edges, often returning to the same perching spots on branches or rocks that feel warm from sun exposure

idTips.label: Medium build
idTips.description: Noticeably stockier than darner dragonflies but more robust than smaller skimmers, with a body that feels substantial if gently handled

habitat: Ski-tipped emeralds favor wooded streams, small rivers, and forest ponds with clean, flowing or well-oxygenated water. They're often found along shaded waterways where overhanging trees create dappled sunlight, and they seem to prefer areas with rocky or gravelly bottoms rather than muddy substrates.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, but early season individuals may be difficult to spot as they're often still maturing and staying in sheltered areas away from water.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs in mid to late summer when adults are actively patrolling territories, mating, and laying eggs - this is the best time for reliable identification.
seasonality.fall: Some individuals may persist into early fall, but they become increasingly scarce and less active as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Adults are absent; larvae overwinter in stream sediments and will not be visible to casual observers.

funFact: The ski-tipped emerald's larvae can take up to three years to develop underwater, spending most of that time burrowed in stream bottom sediments where they ambush prey by shooting out an extendable lower lip that works like a lightning-fast harpoon.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other emerald dragonflies in the same genus, but the male's ski-shaped tail appendages are unique - if you can get close enough to see the tail end clearly, no other emerald has appendages quite like little curved skis.
compareHints: Among its emerald dragonfly relatives, the ski-tipped emerald is distinguished primarily by those characteristic curved male appendages that give it its name. While other Somatochlora species like the clamp-tipped emerald have differently shaped appendages (clamp-like rather than ski-like), and the brush-tipped has bristly appendages, only the ski-tipped has that distinctive upward curve. The overall body size and coloration are quite similar across the genus, making the appendage shape the key distinguishing feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the many Somatochlora emeralds in New England, the Clamp-tipped stands out for its distinctive male appendages that look like mechanical clamps rather than the brush-like, curved, or pointed appendages of its relatives.
Among New England's many Somatochlora species, the brush-tipped emerald is most reliably distinguished by the male's unique claspers that flare outward like brush bristles.
Among its Somatochlora relatives, the Mocha Emerald is unique for its brownish coloration - most other species in this genus display bright metallic greens and blues.
